Normally a date, YYYY-MM-DD in America/Los_Angeles, but a free-text value such as "before 2026-08-20 (confirmed live on the grid)" or "2026-08-20 (concept collision, not scheduled)" counts as used just the same. posts.headline: The kip is a skill not a shortcut
posts.concept: kipping is a different movement not an easier one, earn strict pull-ups first
posts.alt: A man pulls his chin over a pull-up bar on a gym rig with his legs bent behind him.
posts.caption:
Kipping gets called cheating by people who have never tried to do it well. 🤸 It is a different movement, not an easier one.

A strict pull-up is a strength test. A kip is a coordination problem: hollow to arch, then drive the hips and let the bar come to you. Done right it lets you string reps together in a workout without your lats quitting on rep four. Done wrong it is a shoulder injury with a countdown on it, which is the real argument against it.

The order is what matters. Earn a handful of strict pull-ups first so the shoulder has something holding it together, then learn the swing on its own before you add the pull.

Which came first for you, strict or kipping?
posts.first_comment: The hollow and arch swing is worth practicing cold, before you are tired and reaching for reps. How many strict ones can you do right now?

posts.posted_on: before 2026-08-20 (confirmed live on the Instagram grid)
posts.headline: Easy weeks are on purpose
posts.concept: planned deload weeks, adaptation happens when load comes down
posts.alt: A man sits inside a gym rig with his hands clasped and head down, catching his breath between sets.
posts.caption:
An easy week is not falling off. 🗓️ It is the part of the plan most people skip, and then they wonder why month three feels like wading through mud.

Training makes you tired before it makes you strong. The adaptation lands when the load comes down, not while it is going up. Push hard for three or four weeks, then take one where you cut the volume roughly in half and leave a couple of reps in the tank on every set. You are not losing that week. You are collecting on the previous three.

The tell is simple. When your warmup weights start feeling heavier than your working weights used to, you are overdue.

When did you last take one on purpose rather than because life forced it?
posts.first_comment: Forced rest weeks and planned ones do the same thing physically, but only one of them leaves you feeling like you are behind. What does your fourth week usually look like?

posts.posted_on: before 2026-08-20 (confirmed live on the Instagram grid)
posts.headline: Heat is a training variable
posts.concept: heat acclimation, train by effort not by the number on the board in summer
posts.alt: A man in a black shirt and shorts runs toward the camera across a sunlit parking lot outside the gym.
posts.caption:
Training in a Nevada summer is not the same workout you did in March. 🌡️ Same weights, same reps, completely different demand.

Heat is a load. Your body pushes blood toward the skin to cool you, which means less of it reaches working muscle, so your heart rate climbs at a pace that felt easy eight weeks ago. That is not you losing fitness. That is thermoregulation taking its cut. Acclimating takes roughly one to two weeks of consistent exposure and it is real: better sweat response, more blood volume, lower heart rate at the same effort.

Until then, go by effort instead of the number on the board, start hydrated rather than catching up mid session, and take the pace off the first round.

How much slower does summer make your usual pace?
posts.first_comment: Going out at your spring pace in July is the fastest way to blow up in round two. Do you shift to earlier sessions in summer, or just accept the slower splits?

posts.posted_on: before 2026-08-20 (confirmed live on the Instagram grid)
posts.headline: Feeling good is not a prerequisite
posts.concept: how you feel before a session is a poor predictor of the session, let the first set decide
posts.alt: A young man sits on a rowing machine with his head down and forearms on his knees, resting between intervals.
posts.caption:
You will not feel good going into most of your best sessions. 😮‍💨 That is not a motivation problem. It is just what training feels like from the inside.

The days you feel sharp and the days you feel flat produce more similar work than you would guess. People hit lifetime numbers on days they nearly stayed home, and have forgettable sessions on days they felt unstoppable. Your read on your own state before the warmup is close to worthless as a predictor.

So stop using it as one. Warm up, do the first set, then decide. Most of the time the first set answers the question for you.

What is the best session you have had on a day you did not want to be there?
posts.first_comment: The warmup is the honest test, not how you felt in the parking lot. How often does your first set change your mind?

posts.headline: Scaling is not backing off
posts.concept: scaling changes the load not the stimulus, the written weight is a starting point
posts.alt: A man and a woman stand talking in front of a gym whiteboard covered in the day's written workout, with a bench and a water jug beside them.
posts.caption:
The board says 95/55. 🏋️ That number is a starting point, not a verdict on you.

Scaling changes the load, not the stimulus. If the workout is built to leave you breathing hard in eight minutes, using a weight you can actually move gets you there. Grinding the written weight for twenty minutes does not.

What is one movement you scale every single time?
posts.first_comment: A coach is not lowering the bar for you, they are aiming the workout at what it was built to do. What do you wish you had asked a coach sooner?

posts.headline: The carry is the most useful lift
posts.concept: loaded carries build grip midline and shoulders at once and transfer directly to daily life
posts.alt: A man in a purple shirt holds a large black bumper plate against his chest with both hands, shot close so the plate fills the frame.
posts.caption:
Nothing in your day looks like a bench press. 💪 Plenty of it looks like carrying something heavy across a parking lot.

Loaded carries build grip, midline and shoulders at the same time, and they are hard to do with bad form because the weight tells you immediately. Pick something heavy, walk fifty feet, set it down. Three or four trips at the end of a session is plenty.

What is the heaviest thing you carried this week that was not in a gym?
posts.first_comment: Suitcase carries, loaded on one side only, will find an oblique weakness fast. Do you train grip on purpose or just hope it keeps up?

posts.headline: It is a friction problem not a willpower problem
posts.concept: count the decisions between you and the door, remove them the night before instead of recruiting willpower
posts.alt: An empty CrossFit gym before opening at dawn, a gym bag and jump rope set out on a plyo box near the rig, with the words IT IS NOT WILLPOWER stencilled on the bay door, FRICTION in rusted steel letters bolted to the pull-up rig, and Pack the bag tonight painted on the floor.
posts.caption:
Count the decisions standing between you and the gym door. 🚪 That number predicts your attendance better than how motivated you feel.

Missing a session is rarely one big act of quitting. It is six small ones. Where are my shorts. Is my water bottle clean. Do I have time to stop for coffee. What am I even training today. Every one of those is a fork in the road at five in the morning, and your brain is not at its sharpest defending the plan at that hour. Six forks is six chances to take the exit.

So cut the forks down to one. Bag packed the night before and sitting by the door or already in the truck. Shoes in the bag, not by the couch. Know what you are training before you go to sleep, even if it is just the word squats. When the only remaining decision is go or do not go, most people go. 💪

What is the one thing you always end up hunting for on the way out the door?
posts.first_comment: The bag by the door works because it moves the decision to eight at night, when you are rested and reasonable, instead of five in the morning when you are neither. Where does your bag actually live between sessions?

posts.headline: Water is not the same thing as hydration
posts.concept: sweat carries sodium out with the water, plain water replaces volume but not what left with it
posts.alt: A shaker bottle, a tin of coarse salt and a sliced orange staged on a plyo box in a CrossFit gym at golden hour, with A GALLON OF WATER chiseled into the cinder block wall, STILL FLAT carved into stone in electric blue, and Sweat takes salt too painted on the floor.
posts.caption:
You can drink a gallon of water in an August session and still feel flat by the third round. 💧 The water was never the whole problem.

Sweat is not distilled. It carries sodium out with it, and how much varies a lot from one person to the next. Somebody who finishes a hot hour with white crust on the brim of their hat is losing considerably more than somebody whose shirt dries clean. Drink only plain water against that and you top the volume back up without replacing what went out with it, which is part of why the last twenty minutes can feel heavier than the first.

None of that calls for anything exotic. Salt your food like a normal person, and on the long hot ones consider putting something with sodium in the bottle instead of straight water. Your shirt after a session is a decent rough gauge of which camp you are in. If you have blood pressure or kidney considerations, that is a conversation with your doctor rather than something to sort out from a caption. 🧂

What does your shirt look like after an afternoon session in August?
posts.first_comment: The white crust on a hat brim after a hot session is dried sodium, which is why two people can drink the same amount and feel completely different at the end. Do you put anything besides water in the bottle when it is over a hundred out?

posts.headline: Overhead strength is the one you use without noticing
posts.concept: pressing overhead is the pattern behind top shelves and truck beds, and the first one people lose when they stop training it
posts.alt: Chalked forearms lock a loaded barbell out overhead against a fiery sunset in an open gym bay door, with IT IS NOT VANITY stencilled on the door, OVERHEAD in charred timber letters glowing orange, and Top shelves. Truck beds. painted on the wall.
posts.caption:
The strength you actually use most is measured above your head, not off the floor. 🙌 Nobody notices it until it is gone.

Putting something overhead asks three things to cooperate at once: shoulders that can get there, a midline that does not let your ribs flare, and enough strength to finish the last few inches. That combination is what a suitcase into an overhead bin is, what a bag of feed into a truck bed is, what a box onto the top shelf of the garage is. It is also the first pattern to quietly disappear, because a normal day at a desk or a wheel never once asks you to reach straight up.

Keeping it is not complicated. Press something overhead once or twice a week and mean it. Strict press with a barbell, dumbbells, a single kettlebell, even walking the length of the floor with a plate locked out. Go lighter than your ego suggests for the first few weeks, because shoulders pay you back for patience and charge you for hurry. 🏋️

What is the last thing you lifted over your head that was not in a gym?
posts.first_comment: Quick check: stand with your back flat to a wall and raise both arms straight overhead without letting your ribs pop forward. Plenty of strong people cannot, and that is usually mobility rather than strength. How does that one feel for you?

posts.headline: A missed lift tells you where you are weak
posts.concept: the point where the bar slows is diagnostic, train that specific position instead of just adding attempts
posts.alt: A loaded barbell abandoned on the safety arms of a squat rack under cold storm light in a CrossFit gym, with WHERE IT STALLS painted on the rack upright, STICKING POINT in cracked clay letters glowing red, and That is the assignment stencilled on the wall.
posts.caption:
A missed lift is not bad luck. 🔎 It is the most specific piece of information you will get all week, and most people throw it away.

The bar does not slow down at random. It slows in the exact position you are weakest, and that position points at a different job every time. A bench that dies an inch off the chest is a different problem than one that stalls near lockout. A squat that buries you coming out of the bottom is a different problem than one that stops halfway up. Same failed rep, opposite fixes, and adding another attempt next week addresses neither.

So train the spot instead of the lift. Pause a lighter bar for two seconds right where it usually dies. Work partial ranges through that section. Slow the way down so the position gets more time under load. Give it three or four weeks before you decide it is working, because this is the sort of thing that looks like nothing until it suddenly is not. 💪

Where does your worst lift usually die?
posts.first_comment: Filming one heavy set from the side is the cheapest diagnostic in the building, because the bar path shows you the stall clearly even when the rep felt like a blur. What did you change last time a lift stalled, and did it actually move?

posts.headline: Boring and repeatable wins
posts.concept: sustainable frequency beats intensity bursts, build the week you can hold on your worst month
posts.alt: A man in a black tank top and tan pants leans forward at the catch on a Concept2 rower, both hands on the handle.
posts._image_note: 2026-08-24: original composite used photos/untitled-31.jpg, which had already been published on 2026-08-20 (out/2026-08-20/slot1.jpg). Brian flagged the repeat. Rebuilt on photos/untitled-32.jpg, same headline, same clay red style. Copy is unchanged; only the image and alt text moved.
posts.caption:
Three days a week for a year beats six days a week for five weeks. 🚣 It is not close, and it is not even a hard comparison.

The five week version ends the same way every time. Something at work runs long, a kid gets sick, and a schedule with no slack in it does not bend, it breaks. Then the restart costs two weeks of feeling like a beginner again. Meanwhile the three day version absorbs a bad week without anybody noticing, because missing one of three still leaves two.

So build the week you can hold on your worst month, not your best one. If your plan only survives when nothing goes wrong, it is not a plan, it is a good mood with a spreadsheet attached.

How many days a week can you actually hold when life gets loud?
posts.first_comment: The test is not whether the week looks impressive on paper, it is whether it survives a Tuesday that falls apart. What does your week shrink to when things get busy?

posts.headline: One cue at a time
posts.concept: a coach corrects one thing per set because attention does not divide, fix the cue furthest upstream
posts.alt: A black and white view across a gym floor, three people standing and talking near loaded barbells under tall arched windows.
posts.caption:
A good coach will watch five things go wrong and mention one. 🗣️ That is not them being polite. That is how learning a movement actually works.

You cannot consciously correct five things at once. Try it and you get worse at all five, because attention does not divide cleanly and the rep falls apart in the middle while you audit it. So you pick the one furthest upstream, usually the one quietly causing two of the others, and let the rest wait their turn. Bracing, or where the knees track, or where the eyes go. One.

This is also why the internet is a rough place to learn a lift. A comment section hands you nine corrections and no order to put them in.

What is the one cue that finally made a lift click for you?
posts.first_comment: Coaches usually hold three or four corrections back on purpose and bring them out over weeks, which is why a lift can feel like it fixed itself. Has a coach ever told you something that only made sense months later?

posts.headline: Slow down the way down
posts.concept: eccentric tempo adds real work without adding weight and cleans up position at the same time
posts.alt: A person lying on a bench presses two black dumbbells overhead inside a gym rig.
posts.caption:
The half of the rep most people rush is the half that builds the most. ⏱️ Lowering the weight is not the rest between reps.

Muscle is under tension on the way down too, and it can handle more load lowering than lifting. Drop the weight fast and you skip straight past that. Take three seconds on the way down instead and the same dumbbells become a different set, because you just added a pile of work without touching the number on the handle. It cleans up form as a side effect, since you cannot bounce out of a position you arrived at slowly.

Fair warning, this makes you sore out of all proportion to how heavy it felt. Start with a set or two, not a whole session.

What lift would you least want to do with a three second lowering phase?
posts.first_comment: Counting out loud is much harder to cheat than counting in your head, which is the entire reason coaches make you do it. Do you actually count tempo, or just try to feel it?

posts.headline: Getting up is a skill
posts.concept: floor to stand is a trainable pattern nobody rehearses until it stops being easy
posts.alt: A man holds a push-up position on the gym floor beneath an American flag and a wall-mounted fan.
posts.caption:
Nobody practices getting up off the floor until the day it stops being easy. 🧍 Then it is not a fitness question anymore, it is an independence question.

Standing up from the ground without a hand on the furniture asks for hip strength, ankle range and a bit of balance all at once, and that particular combination fades quietly in your forties and fifties if nothing is asking for it. Desks and truck seats never ask. The encouraging part is how fast it answers: get down and back up a handful of times a few days a week and it stays yours.

Squats and lunges build the parts. Actually getting down onto the floor and standing back up trains the whole pattern, which is not quite the same job.

When was the last time you sat on the floor for more than a minute?
posts.first_comment: Try it once without using your hands and notice which side you naturally push up from, because almost everybody has a strong side and has never once thought about it. Which way did you go?

posts.headline: Never miss twice
posts.concept: one missed session is noise, the second one rewrites the story, so the session after a miss is the non-negotiable one
posts.alt: Close-up of two hands in wrist wraps gripping the handle of a rowing machine.
posts.caption:
One missed session is nothing. 📆 Two in a row is where it turns into something.

The first miss is just a Tuesday. Weather, work, a sick kid, a flat tire. It leaves no mark on a month. The second one is different, because the story in your head changes from I missed a session to I am off track, and that story is what actually costs people the next six weeks. The habit rarely dies from the absence. It dies from the narration.

So the rule is small and it holds: miss one, fine, but the next one is not optional. It does not have to be a good session either. Twenty minutes and a shower counts as not missing twice.

What is your version of the twenty minute session that keeps the streak alive?
posts.first_comment: The bar for the session right after a miss should be embarrassingly low, because its only job is to stop the pattern from setting. How long did your longest unplanned break end up running?

posts.headline: Learn the hinge before your back asks
posts.concept: the hip hinge is the pattern that protects you picking things up off the floor in daily life, and it is a rehearsed skill not an instinct
posts.alt: Five worn kettlebells lined up on a steel shelf in a gym.
posts.caption:
Most back tweaks do not happen under a barbell. 🔧 They happen picking up a laundry basket, a toolbox or a toddler, with no warmup and no thought at all.

The pattern that protects you there is the hip hinge. Weight travelling back through the hips, back staying flat, knees soft rather than bent like a squat. It is not complicated, and it is also not what most people do by default, which is to round over from the waist and hand the lower back a job it is not shaped for. A kettlebell deadlift teaches it in about ten minutes, and a swing is the same shape at speed.

The point is not that bending over is dangerous. The point is that hinging is a skill, and rehearsed skills are the ones that show up when you are not paying attention.

What is the everyday thing that has tweaked your back before?
posts.first_comment: A dowel or a broom held along your spine is the cheapest way to feel the difference between hinging and rounding, because it stops touching in three places the moment the position goes. Has anyone ever actually coached you through a hinge?

posts.headline: Your memory rounds every number up
posts.concept: keep a log because memory inflates good days and deletes bad ones, last week's real number is the only honest starting point
posts.alt: A chalked gym whiteboard covered in names, weights and times under a single work light late at night, with YOUR MEMORY INFLATES chalked across the top, WRITE IT DOWN in battered acid green plank letters on the rig, and Next week needs it painted on the floor.
posts.caption:
Ask someone what they squatted last Tuesday and watch the number get rounder as they say it. 📓 Nobody is lying. Memory just does this.

It keeps the best set and quietly loses the two ugly ones before it. It remembers that the weight moved and forgets that the last rep took eleven seconds. Six weeks of that and you have a story about your training instead of a record of it, which is a problem, because the only honest place to start next week is what actually happened last week.

Three lines fixes it. Movement, weight and reps, and one word about how it went. Heavy. Easy. Ugly. The whiteboard is the gym's version of this and the notes app on your phone works just as well. The payoff shows up around week six, when you can look back and tell the difference between genuinely progressing and simply attending. 🧱

Do you keep a log, or run on memory?
posts.first_comment: One word about how the set felt is worth more than the weight six weeks later, because it is the only part your memory will not reconstruct in your favour. What is the oldest training number you still remember, and do you trust it?

posts.headline: Everyone counts protein, nobody counts fiber
posts.concept: fiber is the nutrient nobody tracks, most adults run at roughly half the recommendation, and the gap shows up as appetite and digestion rather than on the scale
posts.alt: Black beans, a split avocado, raspberries and dark rye bread staged on a bench beside a rack of black bumper plates in a CrossFit gym at golden hour, with EVERYONE COUNTS PROTEIN across the top, FIBER in eroded blood red letters standing on the floor, and Nobody counts this one below.
posts.caption:
Ask a gym full of people what their protein target is and every hand goes up. 🫘 Ask about fiber and the room goes quiet.

Most American adults land somewhere around 15 grams a day. The general recommendation sits closer to 25 to 38 depending on size and sex, which means a lot of us are running at roughly half. That is not a moral failing, it is just what happens when most of the day's calories come from things that had the fiber processed out of them on the way to the shelf. The cost usually shows up as being hungry ninety minutes after a meal, and as digestion that never quite settles down.

Fixing it is boring in the best possible way. Beans in the chili. Berries on the yogurt instead of the granola. Leave the skin on the potato. Whole grain bread instead of the soft white stuff. Add it gradually rather than all at once and drink water alongside it, because a sudden jump is uncomfortable in a way that will have you quitting by Thursday. 🥣

Anyone dealing with a gut condition should sort this out with their doctor rather than a caption, since the right answer there is genuinely individual.

What is the one high fiber food you actually enjoy eating?
posts.first_comment: A rough gauge: if you cannot name one thing you ate yesterday that had skin, seeds or beans in it, the number was probably low. What does your usual breakfast look like?

posts.headline: You stopped further from failure than you think
posts.concept: people consistently overestimate how hard a set was and leave several reps unused, so naming reps in reserve out loud is the correction
posts.alt: A loaded barbell on the rubber floor beside a rack of black bumper plates with wrist wraps and a belt draped over it at golden hour, with YOU CALLED IT HARD across the top, REPS LEFT chiseled into the cinder block wall with REPS in molten gold, and Usually about four painted on the floor.
posts.caption:
Ask someone at the end of a set how many more they had in them and the honest answer is usually higher than the guess. 🎯 That gap is where a lot of training quietly goes to waste.

When researchers stop people at the point where they say they are done and then talk them into continuing, most find several more reps waiting. The feeling of a set being finished shows up well before the set is actually finished, and it shows up earliest on the movements you like least. That matters because the reps that drive adaptation are the hard ones near the end. Stop four short and you did the warmup portion of the set and skipped the part that pays.

The fix is a number, not more grit. After every working set, say out loud how many reps you had left. Two. Four. None. Then next set, adjust. Most strength work lives well at one to three left, so if your answer keeps coming back as five, the weight or the rep count needs to move. Saying it out loud is the whole trick, because a number is much harder to fool yourself with than a feeling. 🏋️

Which lift do you suspect you quit earliest on?
posts.first_comment: Your estimate gets sharper with practice, and it is usually worst on the exercises you have the least experience with. Do you train closer to the edge on upper body or lower body?

posts.headline: Training with no start time loses to everything that has one
posts.concept: a session that lives as a floating intention gets pushed by anything scheduled, so it needs a booked hour defended the way a work meeting is
posts.alt: An empty gym at golden hour with rings hanging still, a jump rope and water bottle set out on a plyo box and a worn patch of floor under the rig, with SOMETIME TODAY NEVER HAPPENS along the top, BOOK THE HOUR chiseled into the cinder block wall with HOUR in blood red, and Defend it like work below.
posts.caption:
Anything on your calendar beats anything that is only in your head. ⏰ That is the entire reason a nine in the morning meeting you do not care about still happens and a workout you do care about does not.

A floating intention has no edges. It has no start, so nothing has to end for it to begin, which means every request that arrives with a time attached quietly takes priority. By seven at night the intention is still technically alive and completely unspent, and you tell yourself tomorrow. Meanwhile the person who wrote five thirty on Tuesday has already been and gone, not because they wanted it more, but because their version had a beginning.

So give it a start time and treat it like something you would have to actively cancel. Put it in whatever calendar you already look at. Pick the hour you are most reliably free rather than the hour you are most motivated, because motivation is not a scheduling input. And when something asks for that slot, answer the way you would about a meeting: I have something at five thirty, what about after. 🗓️

What time of day do you train most reliably, and did you pick it or did it pick you?
posts.first_comment: The tell is what you say when somebody asks for that hour, because I am busy holds and I was going to work out folds almost every time. Is your training on an actual calendar right now, or just in your head?

posts.headline: The gym goes one direction and life does not
posts.concept: nearly every gym lift runs straight forward and back, but real loads twist, so anti-rotation work is the piece almost nobody trains
posts.alt: A duffel bag and work boots on the rubber floor beside a steel rig and loaded barbell under cold storm light through a half raised bay door, with GYM GOES ONE WAY stencilled on the door, REAL LIFE TWISTS in cracked earth letters with TWISTS in fiery orange, and Train the turn painted on the wall.
posts.caption:
Squat, press, deadlift, row. 🔄 Every one of them travels straight forward and back, and almost nothing you do outside the gym does.

Think about what actually loads you in a normal week. Swinging a bag of feed into a truck bed. Reaching across the back seat to grab a kid's backpack. Shoveling. Carrying something heavy in one hand while you open a door with the other. All of those are twisting or resisting a twist, and most training programs never once ask for it. So you end up strong in one plane and untested in the plane where you are most likely to get caught out.

The fix is not complicated and it does not need a new program. A suitcase carry with weight in one hand only is anti-rotation training whether you call it that or not. So is a single arm overhead carry, a bird dog done slowly, or a plank with one hand tapping the opposite shoulder. Two or three sets tacked onto the end of a session covers it. 🧰

What is the everyday chore that leaves you sore in a place training never does?
posts.first_comment: Carrying a heavy kettlebell in one hand only for fifty feet will tell you more about your midline than a hundred sit ups, because the whole job is refusing to lean. Which hand feels noticeably harder when you try it?

posts.headline: Your body barely notices what you drink
posts.concept: liquid calories do not trigger the fullness signals that chewed food does, so drinks land on top of the day rather than inside it
posts.alt: A shaker bottle, a tall fountain drink cup and a sports drink staged on a stack of black bumper plates in a CrossFit gym at night under a single work light, with IT NEVER REGISTERS across the top, LIQUID CALORIES in charred wood letters with LIQUID glowing acid green, and Hunger never notices painted on the wall below.
posts.caption:
A 500 calorie smoothie and a 500 calorie plate of food do not land the same way. 🥤 One of them leaves you full and the other leaves you looking for lunch.

Fullness is not just a calorie count arriving in your stomach. It comes from chewing, from the stretch of solid food sitting there, and from the slower drip of hormones that follows a real meal. A drink skips most of that. It empties out fast, it barely touches the stretch receptors, and the signal your brain gets back is faint compared to what an equivalent plate of food would send. That is why a large sweet coffee, a bottle of juice and a sports drink can quietly stack up across a day without ever once feeling like eating.

None of this makes drinks the villain. It just means they mostly add to the day rather than replace part of it. So when a drink is genuinely fuel, like something with sodium in it on a long hot session, use it on purpose. The rest of the time, eating the fruit instead of drinking it costs nothing and keeps you fuller for longer. 🍎

What do you drink most days without ever thinking of it as food?
posts.first_comment: Chewing does more work than people give it credit for, which is why a whole orange and a glass of orange juice can feel completely different an hour later. What is the one drink you would not want to give up?

posts.headline: The belt is not the brace
posts.concept: bracing is a low breath held against a tight midsection and the belt is only something to push into, so a belt cannot create pressure you never made
posts.alt: A loaded barbell with a leather belt draped over it on the rubber floor of a CrossFit gym as a fiery sunset burns through the open bay door, with BREATH BEFORE THE BAR across the top, BRACE FIRST chiseled into the cinder block wall glowing electric blue, and Then move the bar below.
posts.caption:
The belt does not hold your back together. 🫁 The air you trapped behind it does, and the belt is just something for that air to push against.

Here is the sequence most people never get taught. Big breath low into the belly and the sides of the ribcage, not up into the chest. Then tighten everything around it like you are about to take a punch. That pressurised drum is what keeps your spine stacked while a heavy bar tries to fold you in half. A belt raises the ceiling on how much pressure you can build, which is exactly why it helps at heavy loads, but it cannot manufacture pressure you never made. Worn over a soft midsection it is a costume, not a tool.

So practise it with nothing on the bar first. Breathe in low, brace hard, and try to hold that while you walk the length of the gym. Then do it under an empty bar. Then keep doing it at every weight, not only the ones that scare you, because a brace you remember at ninety percent and forget at sixty is not really yours yet. If you have blood pressure concerns, that is a conversation with your doctor before you go hunting for heavy singles. 🏋️

At what weight do you actually start thinking about your breath?
posts.first_comment: If you can talk normally partway through a heavy rep, you are not braced, you are just holding a bar. Do you wear a belt, and did anybody ever teach you when to put it on?
